title: Two scales
translation: Court music has two kinds of scale, ryo and ritsu. Gyōsen, a senior priest at Yokawa on Mount Hiei, once told me: "China is a ryo country. It has no ritsu notes. Japan is ritsu only, with no ryo notes."
original: {横川|よがは}の{行宣|ぎやうせん}{法印|ほふいん}が{申|まう}しはべりしは、「{唐土|もろこし}は{呂|りよ}の{国|くに}なり、{律|りつ}の{音|こゑ}なし。{和国|わこく}は{単律|たんりつ}の{国|くに}にて{呂|りよ}の{音|こゑ}なし。」と{申|まう}しき。
literal: What Gyōsen, the Hōin of Yokawa, said was: 'China is a country of ryo; it has no ritsu notes. Japan is a country of ritsu alone and has no ryo notes', he said.

notes.text: {横川|よがは}: one of the three main areas of the great Tendai monastery on Mount Hiei, north-east of Kyoto. The 1925 edition glosses it simply as the Yokawa valley on Mount Hiei.
{法印|ほふいん}: the highest rank for Buddhist priests. The edition gives no further information about Gyōsen.

notes.quote: 呂の国なり、律の音なし
notes.text: {呂|りよ} and {律|りつ}: the two families of scales in court music (gagaku), which came to Japan from China. The text gives no reasons, and Kenkō adds no comment.
{音|こゑ}: the edition's reading. Here 'notes, tones', not 'voice'.

{申|まう}しはべりしは … と{申|まう}しき: 'what he said was … he said'. The verb comes twice, which is common in reported speech. き: the past for something the writer experienced himself. Kenkō heard this from Gyōsen in person.
